To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PTH‐like peptide (PTH‐rP) was detected by immunohistochemical staining in 100% samples of squamous cancer, in one of six breast carcinomas, in two of three small cell lung carcinomas, and in four of four renal cell carcinomas.
PTHrP can be detected in normal skin and in a variety of cancers by immunoperoxidose staining with a PTHrP antiserum that does not cross react with PTH.
PTHrP is a 17,000‐dalton peptide, the amino acid sequence of which has been determined.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method for the immunohistochemical detection of parathyroid hormone (PTH)-related protein (PTHrp) in histological sections of normal skin and tumors.
the role of PTHr in the development and progression of cancer, and in the development of new therapeutic approaches for the management of hypercalcemia in cancer patients.
the development of an assay for parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHr), which is a polypeptide of 139 amino acids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PTHrP is a useful marker for squamous cell carcinoma and is also found in a proportion of small cell carcinoma and melanoma.
parathyroid hormone related protein is not a general tumor marker.

PTHrP was detected in 100% (n = 34) of squamous cell carcinomas, in 4 of 4 renal cell carcinomas, and in 3 of 3 small cell lung carcinomas, but in only one (16%) of 6 breast cancers and in none of 15 adenocarcinomas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PTHrP may be a marker for squamous cell cancers and that it may have a role in the hypercalcemia associated with some tumors.
PTHrP is a marker of squamous cell differentiation and that it may be involved in the pathogenesis of squamous cell carcinoma.
PTHrP is a useful diagnostic marker for squamous cell carcinomas, and that it may be of diagnostic and therapeutic value in the treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PTHrP is not a tumor‐specific antigen.
PTHrP may be a useful marker in distinguishing squamous cell carcinomas from poorly differentiated adenocarciomata, but that its presence is no more common in the latter group than in normal skin.
PTHrP is expressed in a wide variety of human cancers, including those that are not associated with hypercalcemic syndromes.
